HEADLINE: Better than boot camp
TEXT:
Destinations to kickstart a healthy year.

Many people make resolutions to exercise more and follow a healthy diet at the beginning of a new year, but sticking to those goals is easier said than done.

This year, however, several new fitness-focused retreats in photogenic destinations could help give travellers the motivation they need for lasting success.

Deprivation isn't the point of these getaways. Instead of calorie-restricted diets and hours of punishing workouts, they emphasise balance, a sense of place and, most important, pleasure. In fact, at most, imbibing isn't off-limits - it is even encouraged.

ToneEscapes, for one, is a new company offering five small group retreats during the year in locales such as Marbella in Spain, Santorini in Greece and Saint Lucia in the Caribbean. Company founder Mantas Zvinas, a certified personal trainer and yoga instructor in New York City, says the trips are meant to be the opposite of a boot camp.

"I want to teach people a sustainable lifestyle where you work out moderately and absolutely enjoy a glass or two of wine and reasonable portions of sweets," he says.

Like all ToneEscapes retreats, the one in Marbella, from March 23 to 29, will have morning workouts that incorporate the surrounding environment, such as bike rides along the Andalucia Coast and hikes through the Sierra de las Nieves mountains.

Afternoons will include visits to historic villages and meeting local olive oil and wine producers. Meals will emphasise the abundance of seafood and produce in the area, and local wine will be served at lunch and dinner. Prices start at $US3900 ($5140) a person, inclusive of accommodation, meals, workouts, excursions, activities, local transportation and one spa treatment.

AKT Retreats, for women only, is another choice. Anna Kaiser, a certified personal trainer and the owner of the New York City workout studios AKT, has created four 2018 trips with the purpose of teaching participants how to develop lifelong healthy habits in a fun setting. One retreat, in Nicaragua from May 6 to 11, for example, will include morning workouts that incorporate interval classes, volcano hikes and kayaking in the Pacific Ocean.

Afternoons feature cooking classes on Nicaraguan cuisine and sightseeing tours. Meals will highlight local ingredients.

Prices start at $US3200 a person, inclusive of accommodation, meals, workouts, excursions, local transportation and one spa treatment.

WearActive will lead week-long fitness retreats in the Austrian Alps all year. Guests stay in a private home and can design their own schedule. Activity options include skiing, snowboarding and snowshoe hiking in winter, mountain biking, hiking and rock climbing in summer and yoga during both seasons. An in-house chef prepares all meals. Prices start at €880 ($1240) a person, inclusive of accommodation, most meals, activities and transfers.

38 Degrees North will host three-night active getaways throughout the year in Ibiza and Marbella. Workouts include beach runs, hikes and sunset yoga classes while group sessions with a nutritionist are also part of the itinerary. Prices start at €1300 a person, inclusive of accommodation, most meals, workouts and some activities.

HEADLINE: No alcohol, lots of flavour
TEXT:
Seedlip Garden 108 and Spice 94 [UK]

I like the Seedlip Garden 108, with its punchy green aromatics of herbs and snappy pea-pod (try this in a Martino, with verjuice and dash of olive brine), but I think I prefer the Spice 94, with its complex woody spice fragrance and citrusy quality. When drunk on their own, both taste oddly empty - the lack of richness and body that the alcohol usually brings to spirits is noticeably lacking - but filling this space with a mixer brings them back into balance. $50 seedlipdrinks.com

Sobah Badha Gali pilsner and cerveza [Tweed Heads]

The Sobah name is a play on the word "sober" and a nod to the Yugambeh language of south-east Queensland, which uses "bah" as a suffix indicating place. Badha Gali means "bitter drink" in Gamilaraay language. There are two styles of lager available: lemon aspen from far north Queensland brings a fresh yellow citrusy flavour to the pilsner while finger limes from northern NSW add a greener citrus tang to the cerveza. $7 pozible.com/project/sobah-non-alcoholic-beverages

HEADLINE: Just the tonic
TEXT:
Tipples without the hangover.

Look, I know the topic of non-alcoholic drinks is probably the last thing on your mind at this festive time of year. But I thought you might want to hear about two new booze-free products - one brewed, one distilled - just in case you do wake up one morning over the next few days and think to yourself, "That's it, I am never drinking alcohol again."

The first, Seedlip, a range of two alcohol-free English "spirits", has been around for a couple of years but has only recently arrived in Australia.

The second, Sobah, is a range of non-alcoholic craft beers brewed in Tweed Heads. It has just been launched following two years of product development and a successful Pozible crowdfunding campaign.

"I don't drink alcohol," says Seedlip founder Ben Branson. "But every time I asked for something without booze in it in a bar, I was either given a soft drink or a non-alcoholic beer that tasted terrible. Which is mad - we can put a man on the moon and invent driverless cars but we can't make a good non-alcoholic drink?"

Determined to address this problem, Branson came across a 17th-century book that included techniques for non-alcoholic distillation - mainly for herbal remedies - and started experimenting in his kitchen.

Four years later he is selling two drinks in the Seedlip range, the herbaceous Garden 108 and the exotically perfumed Spice 94, with more in development.

Both have been embraced by bartenders around the world and Distill Ventures, backed by drinks giant Diageo, has taken a minority share in the company.

"We're social creatures," says Branson. "We want to feel we're a part of a group. So, if there's someone who's not drinking for whatever reason in a group of friends enjoying cocktails, this way they can feel like they still belong."

Sobah founder Clinton Schultz is a Gamilaraay man who works as a health and organisational psychologist in the Aboriginal health sector. He also runs an Indigenous food truck business, Clinto's Kupmurri, with his wife Lozen.

"I stopped drinking three years ago," Schultz says. "I'd started cutting down before that because of working in the drug and alcohol rehab space. I'd seen the damage it causes to people and families and communities, and it felt hypocritical to still be drinking myself. Then one Christmas Eve my kids said, 'Dad, stop drinking silly drink,' so I did."

Schultz soon felt the health benefits of being sober, but he missed the flavour of beer. Like Ben Branson, he became frustrated that he couldn't find good-tasting adult non-alcoholic alternatives so he started researching and experimenting with the local Pickled Pig brewery.

After a couple of years Schultz fine-tuned a method of fermenting using a special yeast strain that produces full-flavoured beer with less than 0.5 per cent alcohol.

The timing is good for high-quality booze-free drinks. As consumers in affluent countries around the world embrace the trend for health and wellness, brewers are rushing to respond with low- or no-alcohol beer.

The world's biggest beer company, AB InBev (Budweiser, Corona, Foster's, etc), has announced it intends to have no-and-low brands make up 20 per cent of its global production by 2025. And earlier this year Heineken launched a non-alcoholic version of its famous brand of lager in Europe.

Seedlip and Sobah are also tapping into the trend for local ingredients, with Seedlip including peas and hay in the distillation process to bring an English pastoral quality to Garden 108. Sobah's two beers are flavoured with lemon aspen from far north Queensland and finger limes from Bundjalung country in northern NSW.

For Branson, developing Seedlip is a way of reconnecting with his family's 300-year farming background.

"I get excited by working with my farm, growing some of the ingredients that we use in the distillation," he says.

But he's also keen to establish Seedlip as the first product in a new global category (non-alcoholic distilled drinks) that has the potential for enormous growth. Branson is delighted that his brand has grown faster in its first two years than other notable drinks launched recently, such as Fever-Tree tonic water and Hendrick's gin.

For Schultz, building Sobah into a profitable business is also about rethinking the culture of drinking.

"The long-term goal is to be successful enough to launch a social enterprise fund called Sobah Initiative," he says. "To do drug and alcohol work in a different way - more spiritual and cultural. I'm not against people enjoying a drink - but I am against the normalisation of people being blotto and the reinforcement of needing alcohol to socialise."L&L

As consumers embrace the wellness trend, brewers are rushing to respond.
